scenario: AITA for asking my boyfriend to pick up and drop off my child on weekends which made him suggest a break up? | So for full disclosure my partner works full time and is usually at work from 7am-7pm, and I have a weekend job that requires me to be away from 9am-12pm. We don’t live together but we are local so we are always in and out of each other’s homes. My son decided he wanted to play football on weekends- he’s 12 years old and really excited about it. I was initially going to ask my bf if he could pay for it but I mentioned it to my mum when I went around for a cup of tea and she was strongly expecting me to pay and told me it was my responsibility not my bf’s... even though he’s been in my life 3 years. So I ended up having to pay but in order to afford it I extended my hours at work to 9-5. I asked my bf if he’d be willing to pick up and drop off my son on weekends as obviously if be at work and he looked uncomfortable and said sorry no can’t his dad drop him? I admit I snapped at him and told him that his dad lives in south London whereas we live in north London and his dad doesn’t drive but my boyfriend does. I asked him if he really wanted to be part of this family and if he did he wouldn’t mind doing small stuff like this for me. I suppose his dad COULD take him but what would be a 1 hour + journey for his dad would take 15 minutes for my bf. He got really angry and told me that he was having to work longer hours to support me and my son and that he wanted to use his weekends to go to football games etc as I wasn’t at home anyway. He said that he wanted to chill and relax and that I was forcing things on him way too quick. He then suggested that we break up bc ”I was putting too many responsibilities on him” and I was like.. really? Over a bloody football game? Welcome to the real world love! The little sneak then went over to see my mum and had a heart to heart with her which ended up in HER calling ME and her telling me I am out of line. Who is TA? AITA?

Do your family members rely on your physical presence (e.g., aging parents, siblings in crisis)? - Or is it about emotional proximity? (e.g., "I’d miss family gatherings" vs. "I’m their only emotional support"). *→ Distance doesn’t always equal disconnection. Could you visit often? prediction.raw: 1 **Why?** - **You’re asking him to take on parental responsibilities without him being the parent.** While he’s been in your life for 3 years, he is not your child’s biological or legal guardian. The primary responsibility for transportation falls to you (the parent) or the child’s other parent (his dad), even if inconvenient. Expecting your boyfriend to act as a full-time taxi service for your child—especially when he’s working long hours and has no obligation to do so—is unreasonable. - **You pressured him emotionally.** Saying, *“if he really wanted to be part of this family, he wouldn’t mind doing small stuff like this”* frames his refusal as a lack of commitment, which is unfair. Relationships require mutual consent, not guilt-tripping. If he’s uncomfortable, *that’s his boundary to set*. - **You ignored his perspective.** He’s working longer hours to support you financially, yet you dismissed his need for weekend rest as “not caring.” His desire for downtime is valid—especially when he’s already contributing in other ways. - **The dad’s situation isn’t your problem to solve.** His dad living far away and not driving doesn’t shift the burden to your boyfriend. You and your ex-partner need to co-parent (e.g., arranging carpools, adjusting schedules, or accepting the inconvenience). It’s not his role to fix your co-parenting challenges. **The breakup suggestion was extreme**, but *your request* crossed a line. Healthy relationships require clear boundaries and respect for each other’s limits—not assuming your partner will automatically shoulder your parental duties. If you want him to be more involved, *ask collaboratively* (e.g., “Would you be open to helping sometimes?”), not demand it as a condition of love. > 💡 **Key takeaway**: Being “part of the family” doesn’t mean accepting undefined responsibilities. True partnership means respecting each other’s roles and boundaries—not forcing them.
